title: Food is Brahman
hookLine: right after Bhrigu reaches bliss, the Upanishad walks back into the kitchen: food is Brahman, so honor it, make plenty, and turn no guest away
carry: food is brahman: offer it, share it
tomorrow: the song of one who knows
last: BRAHMAN: WHAT ALL IS BORN FROM AND RETURNS TO.

lines: BLISS IS BRAHMAN. ROLL THE CREDITS?
cards: You'd expect a story like Bhrigu's to end at the summit. He's found it: bliss is Brahman. Cue the light, roll the credits.

Instead, the very next lines of the Taittiriya come straight back down the mountain and into the kitchen. The first thing Bhrigu found, food, the answer that looked too simple, gets the last word. And it's not a vision.
It's a set of house rules: four short vows about eating, sharing and feeding strangers.

teach.h: DO NOT DESPISE FOOD. THAT IS THE VOW.
teach.b: Section seven begins: annam na nindyat, tad vratam. Do not despise food. That is the vow.
Then it explains, in pairs. Breath is food, and the body is the eater of food. The body rests on breath, breath rests on the body.
Each is food for the other. Section eight: do not reject food. Water is food, and fire is the eater.
Section nine: make food plentiful. Earth is food, and space is the eater. Everywhere you look, something is feeding something else, and being held up by it.
That's why food is Brahman here. Not a metaphor for something higher. The chain of eating and being eaten is the same chain Bhrigu traced: what beings are born from, live by, and go back into.
Anna simply means food, what is eaten.
And an earlier verse in the same Upanishad plays on the word: food is eaten by beings, and it eats them in turn, which is why it's called anna.
Then section ten puts it into one rule a household can keep.
Never turn away anyone who comes asking for a place to stay. So, the text says, gather plenty of food, by whatever means you have. Then you can say to a guest, food is ready.
You heard last week, honor the guest as god.
Here's the kitchen behind it. In Hindu homes and temples, food is often offered first and received back as prasad, a gift. Some chant a verse of the Gita before meals.
Either way, the plate isn't neutral. It's Brahman. And that's why so many Hindu temples feed whoever walks in, free: anna-dana, the gift of food, counted among the greatest gifts.

how: Many Hindus offer food to the deity before eating and receive it back as prasad; feeding guests and the hungry (anna-dana) is counted among the great gifts, and many households and temples serve free meals.

o: a fast kept before eating with guests
food offered, then received back as a gift
a verse chanted before every meal

games.q: the eater and the eaten — tap the pairs.

s: after Bhrigu reaches bliss, the Upanishad leaves food behind
it comes straight back: do not despise food. that is the vow.
the text tells a household never to turn away someone seeking shelter
so gather plenty of food, and say: food is ready.
the text says food is eaten and also eats beings
an earlier verse plays on the word anna: it is eaten, and it eats them in turn.

games.q: a stranger knocks at night, asking for a place to stay. you weren't expecting anyone. what does the Taittiriya say?
o: send them on; your food is for your family.
never turn them away, so keep plenty of food.
ask them to come back in the morning.
games.why: section ten: never turn away anyone who asks for lodging. so gather plenty of food, and say, food is ready.

practice: Feel a breath come in: the text calls breath food and the body its eater, so notice the body taking it in, and the breath holding up the body, each resting on the other.
Then widen it to the floor holding you up, the air in the room, the light on your skin, something feeding something else everywhere, and rest inside that chain.

wordCard.voice: Prasad, food offered and given back as a gift. The Taittiriya's vow: do not despise food, for everything eats and is eaten, so honor the plate, make plenty, and never turn away a guest.

orig.note: Sanskrit: "do not despise food." the first of four food vows, Taittiriya 3.7.

carryVoice: Your line: food is brahman: offer it, share it. That's day three hundred ninety-seven.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.8–3.10 (the food vows; no guest turned away)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.2 (food is eaten and eats beings; hence anna)
